claim: show it once, it is learned permanently and everywhere, and that solves any computer use
verdict: The claim holds at clauses 1, 2 and 4 and fails at 3: the lesson is kept, it reaches an unseen function of the same shape, a harmful version of it is refused -- and the very behaviour it teaches is invisible to the project's own tests, which never probe the boundary value. Permanence here is granted to a change the check could not have refused. Clause 5 is not measured at all.

rows.clause: 1. A change shown once is kept
rows.does_not_say: that the change is right, or where it applies

rows.clause: 2. The lesson transfers to an unseen function
rows.evidence: the rule rewrote an unseen function into exactly the intended fix
rows.does_not_say: that it transfers to a different SHAPE or language

rows.clause: 3. The check can tell a right change from a wrong one here
rows.evidence: 1 of 2 sites licensed; the boundary in question is NOT among them; perturbing it to ['<'] changed no passing test
rows.does_not_say: that the check would accept the RIGHT change -- it says it can disagree

rows.clause: 4. Permanence is safe: a wrong lesson is refused
rows.evidence: REJECT (it would have broken a correct program); rows left in the store: 0
rows.does_not_say: that the victims chosen were the right victims -- a gate is bounded by its inputs

rows.clause: 5. The same trick covers anything on a computer
rows.evidence: NOT MEASURED: this tree has no computer-use surface that executes real applications, and a stub would prove nothing

what_would_change_the_answer: a second demonstration from a different place, so the rule varies where it must
a check that reaches the changed file and fails on a mutation of it (clause 3)
an execution surface with rollback and a success predicate, for clause 5
